answers.primary: A remote MCP server connection to the vendor's hosted endpoint over the HTTP (streamable) transport, using the MCP OAuth authorization-code flow so each engineer signs in through their own browser and the client stores a per-user token. Registered once (for example via a committed project-scoped config or a plugin-bundled MCP entry) so every engineer gets the same server definition but their own credential.
answers.rejected_alternative: A local stdio MCP server (or a Bash-invoked vendor CLI wrapped in a skill) reading a shared long-lived API key from an environment variable, which is exactly the shared-secret model the team wants to avoid.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The MCP client owns transport, the OAuth handshake, token storage and refresh, and it decides which tools are exposed; the model only sees tool schemas and results and cannot bypass or forge the credential.
answers.context_boundary: The server runs as a remote process outside the session. Tool definitions and tool results cross into the main session context window; the browser sign-in and the resulting token never appear in the transcript, so pasted stack traces are replaced by scoped tool responses.
answers.lifecycle: The server is loaded at session start once its config is present and trusted; the first tool use (or an explicit /mcp authenticate step) triggers the browser login, after which the connection lives for the session and the token persists across sessions until it expires or is revoked. It stops applying when the server entry is removed or the plugin/project config is disabled.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on authentication: an unauthenticated or expired token turns every call into a tool error, and the model may fall back to guessing or to asking for a pasted trace. The practical risk is context flooding, since raw error-tracker payloads are large and a single unfiltered query can consume much of the window.
answers.version_caveat: Remote MCP over HTTP with OAuth is a comparatively recent capability and the older SSE transport has been superseded by streamable HTTP; I cannot state the exact minimum Claude Code version or the precise config key names from model knowledge alone. Hosted third-party connectors can also be plan- or admin-gated in managed deployments.

answers.primary: LSP integration: attach a TypeScript language server (tsserver via typescript-language-server) to the session, either through the IDE integration or a plugin-bundled LSP server declaration, so post-edit diagnostics are surfaced automatically and definition/reference lookups become structured calls instead of grep.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PostToolUse hook that shells out to `tsc --noEmit` after every Edit or Write; it can surface type errors but gives no navigation, and full-project typechecking after each edit is far too slow on a real codebase.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The client attaches diagnostics to edit results and serves symbol queries from the language server process without the model having to remember to ask; the model owns only whether it acts on what it is shown.
answers.context_boundary: The language server holds the whole project index in its own process. Only the diagnostics for the touched files and the specific definition/reference results cross into the main session context, which is what keeps this cheaper than grepping the tree.
answers.lifecycle: The server starts when the session opens a matching file or when the plugin declaring it loads, produces diagnostics after each edit, and is torn down at session end. It stops applying if the server crashes, if the project has no resolvable tsconfig, or if the integration is not enabled.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory in the end: diagnostics are injected, but nothing forces the model to fix them before moving on. It fails open, a crashed or slow-to-index server silently yields no diagnostics and the behaviour regresses to the original problem, and on a large monorepo a noisy diagnostic stream can itself eat context.
answers.version_caveat: Native LSP support and plugin-bundled language-server configuration are newer additions to Claude Code; I do not know the minimum version, the manifest key, or whether diagnostics-on-edit requires the IDE extension rather than the CLI alone, so that should be verified against the current docs.

answers.primary: A plugin that bundles all four component types (review subagents, slash commands, hooks, and an MCP server config) distributed through a plugin marketplace, with the marketplace and the enabled plugin declared in each repository's checked-in `.claude/settings.json` so a fresh clone offers the same set. One package, one update channel, many repos.
answers.rejected_alternative: Committing loose `.claude/agents`, `.claude/commands`, `.claude/hooks` and `.mcp.json` files into every repository; it works on first clone but has no update path, so each repo's copy drifts and every change means N pull requests.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns distribution, loading and updating, but the engineer owns acceptance: repository-declared marketplaces and plugins are offered and require a trust or enable decision, they are not silently forced onto the machine.
answers.context_boundary: Loading happens outside the model. Command, subagent and skill metadata is what enters each session's context window; hooks and the configured MCP server run as separate processes, and subagent invocations get their own isolated context whose result alone returns to the main thread.
answers.lifecycle: On a fresh clone the repo settings point at the marketplace and Claude Code offers the plugin; once trusted it loads at every session start in that repo, and updates arrive when the marketplace is refreshed or updated. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled, uninstalled, or the settings entry is removed.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open as a standardisation mechanism: any engineer can decline the trust prompt or disable the plugin, so this distributes capability rather than enforcing it. Secondary failures are a stale marketplace cache delaying updates and name collisions when two plugins ship the same command or subagent name.
answers.version_caveat: Plugins and plugin marketplaces are a relatively recent Claude Code feature and the settings keys for pre-declaring marketplaces and enabled plugins have moved as it matured; I cannot state the exact minimum version or key names from model knowledge, and managed/enterprise policy settings may restrict which marketplaces are allowed.

answers.primary: A plugin that ships the compiled binary and exposes it as a plugin-provided executable, so the harness prepends the plugin's binary directory to the PATH used by the Bash tool. That makes it a bare command available to ordinary pipelines in every project where the plugin is enabled, with no user PATH edits.
answers.rejected_alternative: An MCP server that wraps each subcommand as a tool; it would work, but it destroys shell composability with grep and jq and inflates the tool list with dozens of near-identical schemas.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. It constructs the environment that the Bash tool runs in, so availability of the command is a property of the enabled plugin, not something the model arranges or can be talked out of.
answers.context_boundary: The binary executes in the Bash subprocess, entirely outside the model's context; only the command line the model wrote and the captured stdout/stderr cross the boundary, which is why pipe-and-filter composition keeps output small.
answers.lifecycle: In effect for the whole session whenever the plugin is enabled, resolved per Bash invocation at command lookup time. It stops applying the moment the plugin is disabled or uninstalled, or in a session where the toolkit was never enabled.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed but noisily: without the plugin the command is simply not found, and the model's usual reaction is to improvise an alternative rather than stop. Real-world breakage is a platform or architecture mismatch for a single compiled binary across mac/Linux/Windows shells, and Bash permission rules that deny the command name.
answers.version_caveat: I am not confident of the exact plugin manifest field that registers executables or of the environment variable naming for the plugin root directory, and PATH injection for plugin binaries is a newer capability; both need checking against the installed version rather than assumed.

answers.primary: Distribute the toolkit as a plugin from a git-backed marketplace that tracks a branch head rather than tagged releases, so the marketplace source is the repository itself and every merged commit to the tracked branch becomes the next update teammates receive.
answers.rejected_alternative: Publishing versioned releases (semver bumps in the plugin manifest, or an npm package / GitHub Release per change); it gives clean rollback but reintroduces exactly the release bookkeeping the team wants to eliminate.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The plugin/marketplace updater fetches and installs; the model has no role in the update path and cannot pin, skip or roll back a version on the user's behalf.
answers.context_boundary: Fetching and installing happen outside any model context. Only the resulting components (command, subagent and skill definitions, hook registrations) enter a session's context window, and only from the next session that loads the updated copy.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered by a marketplace refresh or update, typically on install and on an explicit update, tracking whatever is at branch head at that moment. The delivered version applies for the life of a session and stops when the plugin is disabled or the marketplace entry is removed.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and unpinned: a broken commit ships to everyone immediately with no reviewed release gate and no obvious rollback, and there is no per-user version to diagnose against. Sessions already running keep the old copy until restart, so the fleet is briefly inconsistent after each merge.
answers.version_caveat: I cannot state from model knowledge whether updates are automatic on session start or require an explicit update command in the current version, nor the exact marketplace source schema for pinning a branch; branch-tracking behaviour should be confirmed before promising daily delivery.

answers.primary: A local stdio MCP server acting as an authenticating proxy: it invokes the SSO helper command to mint a token, attaches it to each request against the internal HTTP tool service, and re-mints on expiry or on a 401. The proxy is what gets registered as the MCP server, not the HTTP endpoint directly.
answers.rejected_alternative: Registering the internal service directly with the HTTP transport and a static `Authorization` header populated from an environment variable; header values are resolved once at connect time, so the connection dies silently when the short-lived token expires mid-session.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness plus the proxy process own credential freshness. The model never sees, holds or refreshes the token; it only observes tool success or a tool error, which is the correct separation for a short-lived secret.
answers.context_boundary: The proxy runs as a separate local process spawned by the MCP client. Tokens and the SSO helper's output stay in that process; only tool schemas and tool results cross into the session context window.
answers.lifecycle: Starts when the MCP server list loads (session start or first tool use), refreshes per call or on authentication failure for the life of the session, and exits with the session. It stops applying if the server entry is removed or the helper command is unavailable.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed: an expired or unmintable token produces tool errors rather than silent wrong answers, but the model tends to retry in a loop instead of surfacing the auth problem. The nastier case is an SSO helper that wants an interactive prompt, which blocks the stdio process and hangs the whole server.
answers.version_caveat: I cannot confirm from model knowledge whether the current Claude Code MCP config supports a dynamic token or credential-helper command field for HTTP transports; if such a field exists it would remove the need for the proxy, so that should be checked before building one. Environment-variable expansion in MCP config is static and is not a substitute.

answers.primary: Plugin-bundled hooks: a SessionStart hook that launches the log tailer in the background when the toolkit loads, plus a UserPromptSubmit (or equivalent turn-boundary) hook that injects newly appended lines as additional context. Nobody has to ask, because the hook fires from the plugin being active rather than from a model decision.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill or an MCP tool that reads the log, which is the obvious shape but requires the model to decide to call it; nothing would make it poll, so new error lines would go unnoticed until someone asked.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Hooks fire deterministically on their events and the model cannot decline to receive the injected lines, which is precisely why this beats a model-invoked tool for an unprompted stream.
answers.context_boundary: The tail process runs outside the session entirely. Only the delta of appended lines crosses into the main session context window as injected context, so the log file itself never has to be read into the window.
answers.lifecycle: Starts at SessionStart whenever the plugin is enabled, delivers on each subsequent turn boundary, and ends when the session ends and the child process is reaped. It stops applying if the plugin is disabled or the hook errors out.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open: a hook that errors, times out or produces no output is skipped, and the session simply never hears about errors while appearing to work. The delivery is also turn-granular rather than truly instantaneous, and a chatty error log can flood the context window or push out earlier work.
answers.version_caveat: Hook event names and the JSON field used to inject additional context have changed across Claude Code versions, and I cannot state which version introduced the ones used here. I also do not know whether the current version provides a genuine push/streaming channel from a background process into an idle session, which would be the better fit if it exists.

answers.primary: The MCP connection to the hosted integration stays as it is, but the read-only guarantee has to be minted at the vendor's authorization server: a read-only client, role, or scope set so the token issued to each engineer is structurally incapable of writing. Locally, back it with harness permission deny rules on the write tool names as defence in depth.
answers.rejected_alternative: Relying on permission deny rules (or a PreToolUse hook) over the write tool names alone; that constrains this one client on one machine and says nothing about what the stored credential could authorize from anywhere else.
answers.enforcement_owner: Neither the model nor, ultimately, the harness. The harness owns the local layer and can hard-block the tool call, but the binding guarantee the security team asked for lives outside both, in the identity provider that issues the token. The model is not an enforcement point here at all.
answers.context_boundary: Consent and scope selection happen in the browser, out of context. Only the tool schemas the server advertises and the tool results cross into the session; note that write tools may still appear in the schema list even when the token cannot exercise them.
answers.lifecycle: Applied at first connect and consent, and it persists for the token's lifetime, renewing on refresh. Re-consent is triggered if the vendor changes advertised scopes, which is the moment write access could be silently re-requested, so that event needs watching.
answers.failure_mode: The local layer fails open over time: deny rules keyed to tool names go stale when the vendor renames a tool or ships a new write tool, and the block quietly stops covering everything. The token-scope layer fails closed, with the server returning an authorization error the model reports as a tool failure.
answers.version_caveat: I cannot confirm from model knowledge whether the current Claude Code MCP OAuth client supports narrowing requested scopes rather than accepting what the server advertises; assume it does not and put the restriction on the vendor side. Enterprise-managed policy settings, where available, are the right place for the deny rules so engineers cannot relax them.

answers.primary: A project-scoped MCP server declared in a `.mcp.json` committed at the repository root. That is the scope built for exactly this: it travels with the clone, applies only to this repository, and the harness prompts each user once to approve project-scoped servers before they run.
answers.rejected_alternative: A user-scoped server added with the MCP add command at user scope; it would work per engineer but requires manual setup on every machine and leaks the staging-database connection into every other project they open.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. It reads the committed file, gates the server behind the per-user approval prompt, records that choice, and starts the process; the model neither sees nor influences the consent decision.
answers.context_boundary: The server runs as its own process. Its tool definitions and results cross into the context window of sessions started inside this repository only, which is what keeps the connection out of unrelated projects.
answers.lifecycle: First session in a fresh clone triggers the one-time approval prompt; after that it loads on every session in that project. There is a command to reset project MCP approval choices, and it stops applying when the file is removed, the server is disabled, or the user declines.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed before consent, so the tools are simply absent and the model works around them rather than erroring loudly, which can look like the config never landed. Practical failures are declining the prompt, a missing local binary or environment variable referenced by the config, and the temptation to commit a database credential into a tracked file.
answers.version_caveat: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` with a per-user approval prompt and a reset command for those choices has been in Claude Code for a while, but I cannot name the version that introduced it or the exact reset command name from model knowledge. Enterprise policy can also disable project-scoped MCP servers entirely.

answers.primary: Ship the toolkit as a plugin whose dependencies are installed by an idempotent bootstrap step (a SessionStart or install-time hook) that writes `node_modules` into a stable, plugin-named data directory outside the version-stamped plugin install path, guarded by a marker or manifest-hash check so it runs once and re-runs only when the dependency manifest changes.
answers.rejected_alternative: Vendoring `node_modules` into the plugin repository so it arrives with the plugin content; it removes first-run installation but bloats every update, breaks on native modules built for another platform, and still ties the modules to the version-stamped directory.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness runs the bootstrap hook at the right moment, but correctness of the install (idempotency, location, lock detection) belongs to the script the plugin authors write; the model is not involved in either.
answers.context_boundary: The install runs in a subprocess at session start, entirely outside the model's context. Only a short success or failure signal should cross into the session; piping full npm output into context is a common and avoidable waste.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on first run after install and after any update whose dependency manifest differs, then no-ops for every subsequent session. It stops applying on uninstall, and the external data directory then needs cleaning up manually because it deliberately lives outside the plugin's own tree.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open in the worst way: a failed or partial install leaves commands broken while the session starts normally, and the model improvises around missing tools instead of reporting the install failure. The specific breakage the requirement names comes from installing into the version-stamped plugin directory, which strands or wipes the modules at the next update; concurrent sessions racing on the same install directory is the other common one.
answers.version_caveat: I do not know from model knowledge whether current Claude Code plugins expose a dedicated install or post-update lifecycle hook, or a stable per-plugin data directory environment variable; if neither exists, SessionStart with a marker file is the available substitute and the directory path has to be chosen by the plugin author. Plugin directory layout has changed as the feature matured, so do not hardcode it.
